  7. Flexibility: Implementing an adaptable outbound logistics system gives companies clear visibility of disruptions as they take palace, allowing them to plan accordingly and adapt to them. It also gives companies the ability to respond to market fluctuations which could change demand for a product.

  8. Market expansion: By having a good program for outbound logistics, companies can also establish a clear path to reach new markets or quickly deliver new goods through established routes thus gaining broader audiences.

Inbound Logistics Challenges

Inbound logistics present numerous challenges within the realm of supply chains that require effective planning to be overcome. Key aspects such as inventory management, choice of transportation methods, and maintaining strong supplier relationships are all critical in meeting customer demands.

There really is no end to the problems that can emerge from inbound logistics. Issues such as delivery delays, inventory mismanagement, and escalating transportation expenses can significantly impact the efficiency of an entire supply chain. Furthermore, inadequate visibility into the location of inbound shipments and inefficient warehouse operations can further exacerbate these challenges, resulting in bottlenecks in the movement of goods across the distribution network—problems where a product like Desteia can be of immense help.

To address these challenges effectively, companies must streamline their inbound logistics processes through better coordination with suppliers, implementing advanced tracking technologies for shipment visibility, optimizing warehouse operations for faster throughput, and adopting cost-effective transportation solutions—htough the actual order or degree of implementation will vary company to company. By enhancing efficiency and transparency in inbound logistics operations, organizations can boost overall supply chain performance and meet customer expectations more effectively.

Main Inbound Challenges

  1. Supplier delays: Late deliveries disrupt production timelines. Think, for instance, of a factory waiting for raw materials. Without those inputs, the entire production will come to a halt due to delayed shipments.

  2. High transportation costs: A big problem in bound logistics—more so in recent years—has been the drastic shift in transportation costs. This is most commonly attributed to the volatility in fuel prices that results in a direct cost increase to transportation. But, more recently, a number of supply chain disruptions such as the blockade of the Suez Canal by Houthi rebels, have also brought prices up.

  3. Inventory mismanagement: Whenever companies over or understock inputs based on unforeseen demand, they often have to pay additional storage costs or lose sales due to unmet demand.

  4. Quality issues: At times, when companies lack a clear understanding of their suppliers, they could receive low-quality materials which, in turn, affect product quality.

  5. Communication barriers: At times, lacking a clear communication channel with a supplier can result in misaligned expectations between actors that result in further problems. Think of a company ordering paper to a provider to make books without specifying the specific quality. The supplier can assume the company wants a cheap paper, lowering quality but reducing costs, or an expensive paper that has high quality but an equally high cost. If the company is not aligned with either extreme, they could receive paper of unknown quality for their goods and fail to produce their desired product.

  6. Regulatory compliance: Navigating import/export regulations adds complexity to any supply chain and can result in additional costs if handled poorly.

  7. Capacity constraints: Finally, limited warehouse or transport capacity creates bottlenecks in your supply chain that could be difficult to address.

Inbound Logistics Performance Indicators

On-time deliveries, inventory accuracy, and supplier lead times are some crucial factors that indicate the effectiveness of inbound logistics. These key performance indicators (commonly referred to as KPIs) offer insights into the reliability and efficiency of the supply chain. Timely deliveries, for instance, ensure that products reach their destinations promptly and in optimal condition, contributing to customer satisfaction and operational success.

It is worth noting that efficient warehouse operations play a significant role in maintaining inventory accuracy and ensuring that the right amount of stock is available when needed. Pairing this with low-cost transportation options helps streamline inbound logistics processes and minimize costs. 

Overall, monitoring these performance indicators allows businesses to make informed decisions that enhance customer satisfaction, reduce expenses, and promote seamless operations throughout the supply chain.

Furthermore, optimizing inbound logistics not only benefits individual businesses but also strengthens relationships with suppliers and partners. By focusing on improving these aspects of the supply chain, companies can foster trust, improve collaboration, and create a more resilient and competitive business environment.

Main Inbound KPIs

  • Average lead time: Time taken to receive raw materials after placing an order.

  • Freight bill accuracy: Ensures accurate invoicing for shipments without drastic changes upon receiving products.

  • Damaged goods rate: Tracks the percentage of materials damaged during transit.

  • On-time delivery rate: Measures supplier punctuality.

  • Loading and unloading times: Assesses efficiency at docks.

  • Supplier reliability index: Evaluates the consistency of supplier performance.

  • Cost per shipment: Measures the average expense for each delivery.

Outbound Logistics Challenges

Managing outbound logistics, much like their inbound counterpart, poses several challenges that require careful navigation to ensure smooth operations. Timely deliveries, for instance, are crucial to create customer trust, and cost efficiency is equally important in this process to ensure companies are as profitable as possible. Thus, effective outbound transportation plays a pivotal role in meeting customer expectations while keeping expenses in check. 

For such processes to work, coordination with multiple stakeholders is necessary, along with meticulous planning for last-mile delivery solutions. Balancing high service standards with cost-effective shipping methods can be demanding but is essential for overall success.

Optimizing distribution networks and streamlining return processes are ongoing hurdles in outbound logistics management. Addressing these challenges is vital for enhancing customer satisfaction levels and creating the overall supply chain risk management strategy of a company. By implementing strategic solutions and leveraging technological advancements, businesses can overcome these obstacles and create a more efficient and customer-centric outbound logistics framework.

Main Outbound Challenges

  1. Delayed deliveries: Whenever shipments suffer from delays, customers are likely to be disappointed. Afterall, they received an initial promise from a company as to when a product would be at their door.

  2. Transportation costs: Similar to inbound logistics, a big pain for outbound logistics is directly related to the volatile nature of transportation costs. Since the actual price of transportation is dependent on fuel prices and changing carrier fees, companies can often struggle to allot the right budget to said costs.

  3. Order inaccuracies: A major problem in outbound logistics—specifically when companies ship to customers directly—has to do with shipping wrong orders. This can be the result of a difficulty in tracking shipments and matching them to their customers, which, in turn, leads to increased returns and refunds.

  4. Warehouse inefficiencies: When a warehouse is poorly run, companies might struggle to bring in new materials from a factory or even to find the right materials for an order. This slows down order fulfillment and makes companies much less efficient.

  5. Last-mile delivery issues: There are a number of key challenges when delivering to customers directly, most commonly in the form of failing to find an address or reaching a building without the correct numbering to make a delivery.

  6. Technology breakdowns: System failures disrupt real-time tracking and thus result in further complications with deliveries. It is essential to have reliable tools in place to avoid such problems.

  7. Workforce shortages: Finally, having insufficient staff during times of increased demand can affect fulfillment speed of goods and drastically reduce your output.

Outbound Logistics Performance Indicators

Measuring the effectiveness of outbound logistics involves assessing key factors such as on-time delivery, order accuracy, and customer satisfaction. Timely deliveries not only instill trust in a brand but also foster customer loyalty, benefiting the entire supply chain. In sum, accurate orders minimize errors and reduce returns, ultimately enhancing the overall customer experience. Not to mention that monitoring shipping costs and efficiency is essential for cost savings and effective outbound logistics management.

Tracking these metrics allows businesses to optimize their logistics operations, meeting customer expectations and maintaining competitiveness in the market. Additionally, implementing advanced technologies like real-time tracking systems and route optimization software can further streamline outbound logistics processes, ensuring smoother operations and improved customer satisfaction levels. By prioritizing efficiency and customer-centric strategies in outbound logistics, businesses can strengthen their supply chain performance and drive sustainable growth.

Main Outbound KPIs

  • Average delivery time: Measures the speed of order fulfillment from the time a product leaves the factory until it reaches its end consumer.

  • Order accuracy rate: Tracks the share of deliveries that were error-free.

  • Inventory turnover: Indicates how quickly goods are sold—often measured by product.

  • Order fill rate: Measures the percentage of orders that were fulfilled completely.

  • Cash-to-cash cycle time: Refers to the time it takes to convert initial investments in goods into cash flows.

  • Customer satisfaction score: Measures client contentment with deliveries mostly in the form of post-delivery surveys.

  • Delivery route efficiency: Tracks the efficiency of each shipping path used by a company—most frequently by measuring the difference between the ETA and the actual time of arrival.

  • Cost per delivery: Analyzes expenses incurred per shipment.

How Inbound and Outbound Logistics Shape the Supply Chain

In conclusion, it is important to understand the differences between inbound and outbound logistics. Doing so helps businesses improve supply chain efficiency. Knowing the needs of each part of the process allows companies to make their logistics operations smoother and thus increases overall satisfaction and cost savings.

Using effective logistics processes is key to having an efficient inbound and outbound operation. This includes good inbound and outbound transportation methods, efficient inventory management, and building strong relationships with logistics providers. These are all important to meet customer expectations and stay competitive. By focusing on these points, businesses can create a risk mitigation strategy that meets the different needs of the supply chain.

Modern logistics software, such as Desteia, can transform supply chain management by giving better visibility and document management. Desteia’s platform offers real-time tracking, and analytics of carrier and route performance, all while proving a seamless integration experience. This, in turn,  empowers businesses to build efficient and resilient supply chains that meet their expectations.

With Desteia, companies can identify bottlenecks, reduce costs, and enhance transparency throughout the supply chain. If you’d like to see how Desteia can help your company, make sure to schedule a call with our experts in the “Contact us” section of our website.

item.title: Asia to Mexico Shipping Rates: Finding the Best Prices
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.description: Asia-Mexico commerce is on the rise. We looked at current costs to suggest some key strategies to make your routes more efficient.
item.content:encoded:
Mexico is becoming a global hub for trade. As the U.S. and other Western nations seek to replace China as a direct provider, the Latin American nation has become a key destination for foreign capital—a process commonly known as nearshoring. 

A great part of this change has come with an increased number of trade routes that connect Mexico with other developing economies across the globe. Most prominently, with Asia, which recently went from accounting 28.3% of major shipping routes to and from the country to nearly 35%. But just how much does it cost for foreign goods to enter Mexico and what’s the cheapest alternative to do so?

In this essay, we go deeper into understanding how Mexican trade works—how expensive it is and which are the key strategies to make your global operations in Mexico cheaper. We use Asia as a case study since it is both the fastest growing trade corridor for Mexico outside the US border, and one for which maritime data is readily available. This allowed us to aggregate a great number of financial data points to accurately depict the cost of shipping from Asia to Mexico.

More specifically, we are focusing on five ports in particular: Shanghai, Ningbo, Qingdao, Busan, and Hong Kong. These five ports account for a considerable portion of Mexico’s ocean routes. In fact, in a previous research piece for Desteia, we found that Busan was the most connected port to Mexico with 26 routes leading to Mexican ports. Shanghai was the fourth most connected with 19 routes. Adding the other three ports considered in this analysis, we get a total of 83 connections to Mexico via ocean trade.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/NULmn/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Taking these five ports as a reference, we then looked at the current market rates from thirteen ocean carriers. In particular, we looked at the cost of shipping different types of containers to the two largest ports in Mexico: Lazaro Cardenas and Manzanillo. In total, we considered 210 shipping routes connecting these five ports to Mexico. As shown in the diagram below, there was a clear tendency of shipping Chinese cargo to Mexico through Shanghai which accounted for over 50% of all ports considered—not a surprising fact when considering Shanghai is the busiest port in the world. It was followed by Ningbo with 21.9% of routes analyzed and Qingdao with 13.81% of routes.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BZSxG/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

We considered four types of containers for this study: 20ft standard containers (20GP), 40ft standard containers (40GP), 40ft high containers (40HQ), and 40ft non-operational reefers (40NOR). In the figure below, we share the average price for shipping each of these containers from Asia to Mexico. As the graph shows, the cheapest container is the 20dft standard container followed by a 40ft non operational reefer. Not surprisingly, 40ft containers are higher in value as they offer more volume—although, it is worth noting that a 40ft high is the exact same price as a standard 40ft container despite having more volume.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LDoX0/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The above graph also suggests a very important fact about the price of shipping cargo. The price of shipping is not proportional to the volume benign shipped. Although a 40ft container is more expensive as a whole than a 20ft container, they are actually much cheaper when you consider the actual volume. We can extrapolate this from the previous figures. A 40ft container has double the volume of a 20ft container yet it costs just 10% more in shipping fees.

A better way to consider the actual cost of a shipping container from Asia to Mexico would be to look at the dollar value per volume of each container. That is, the USD per cubic meter of each container being shipped from Asia to Mexico. As we show in the figure below, once you consider the volume of each container, it is considerably cheaper to use 40ft containers than 20ft containers. Similarly, it is cheaper to use 40ft high containers than 40ft standard containers as they cost the same but have more volume (67.6 cubic meters vs 76.3 cubic meters).

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/cM2tM/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Data thus far has focused on the abstract routes connecting Asia and Mexico. However, there are great cost savings opportunities if we consider the actual ports being used to ship cargo to Mexico. In the map below, we plotted the average price to ship a container from the top asian ports to Mexico—irrespective of container type. As the map shows, the most expensive origin port when shipping to Mexico is Qingdao with an average cost of $2,100 per container. In second place we find Shanghai with an average cost of $1,870.8 per container, followed by Busan with $1,570.8 per container, Ningbo with $1,525.6, and, finally, Hong Kong with $1,503.6.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/TWNMw/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The above map already has some meaningful insights in terms of potentially favorable routes when shipping from Asia to Mexico. The clearest example would be to ship cargo from Nimgbo rather than Shanghai, since the two ports are close neighbors—less than a two hour drive from one another. Just by shipping from Ningbo instead of Shanghai, a company could save up to $300 per container. A similar argument could be said of shifting cargo from Qingdao to Shanghai or Ningbo which would save $400 or $700 per container respectively—although, Qingdao is eight hours away from Shanghai, likely resulting in considerable transportation fees as a result of the re-route. 

Furthermore, as we saw in terms of aggregate data, there are clear differences in the cost of shipping when considering different container types. In the figure below, we break down the cost of shipping from all five ports considered by container type. Again, we see the same pattern where 40ft containers are slightly more expensive than their 20ft counterparts despite having double the volume. In all cases, it costs the same to ship a 40ft high container and a 40ft standard container.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rXkXx/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

There are also some variations when it comes to the destination port in Mexico albeit to a much smaller degree. In the figure below, we compare the cost to ship cargo from Asia to the ports of Manzanillo and Lázaro Cárdenas in Mexico. As the graph shows, it is slightly cheaper to ship to Manzanillo than Lázaro Cárdenas. However, the difference is so small that it might be offset by transportation costs if Manzanillo happens to be further away from the desired destination. Once more, we see that it is only slightly more expensive to ship using a 40ft container than a 20ft container.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ieiHU/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

We also looked at the difference in costs by carrier. In so doing, we actually found the greatest source of variance for companies shipping cargo. As shown in the figure below, costs in shipping can vary by as much as $1,000. ZIM, the most expensive carrier, had an average cost per container of $2,453.33—irrespective of container type. Meanwhile, YML—the cheapest carrier for Asia-Mexico trade—charges just $1,462.68. 

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3xjHr/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Now, it is worth noting that there is great variance of costs when it comes to the type of container provided by each carrier. In the figure below, we break down the cost to ship a container by its type. Broadly speaking, the pattern where 40ft containers are slightly more expensive than 20ft containers holds for most carriers–only Maersk and WHL break this rule having the same price for both types of containers. However, the price of a non operating reefer varies drastically with come companies like YML charging significantly less while PIL, EMC, ONE, and MSC all charge more.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/AF3oW/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The above research helps understand one of the fastest growing trade corridors in the world: that between Mexico and China. Moreover, it demonstrates that, by looking at aggregate data, companies can better plan for the best route to meet their supply chain needs. As a result, they can find the cheapest container to use or the most cost-effective route for their needs. In the end, it’s all about how you use data to make your logistics operations more efficient.

At Desteia, we believe all operators should have full data visibility when making decisions—be it by structuring internal data or tapping into external data sources. If you’d like to see how better data visibility could help your company, make sure to schedule a call with one of our experts!

item.title: Trump Tariffs Come Into Effect
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.description: President Trump just announced tariffs against its three largest trade partners. We looked at their true impact to the global economy.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has finally announced a series of tariffs against Mexico, China, and Canada—the three largest trade partners of the U.S. This comes after a long series of campaign promises to impose tariffs against the three nations and an initial delay during the month of February. China, Mexico, and Canada have all responded with tariffs of their own against US products, sparking what might well be the largest trade war in modern history.

The tariffs themselves mark a drastic shift in US foreign policy which, for years, was focused on free trade as a core pillar of diplomacy. Moreso with Mexico and Canada which are both members of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)—an ambitious free trade agreement negotiated by President Trump himself that allowed the free flow of products between the three nations. Now, the U.S. has broken with the USMCA by imposing 25% tariffs on all Mexican products and 25% tariffs on all Canadian products with the exception of energy which will have just 10% tariffs.

China, for its own part, received a much smaller set of tariffs than those originally promised by President Trump. Across the campaign trail, then candidate Trump suggested a blanket tariff of 60% on all Chinese goods. After he took office, however, he went for a much more restrained 10% tariff on all Chinese goods during his first month in office and an additional 10% announced with tariffs to Mexico and Canada. This brings tariffs on Chinese products to 20%.

To understand the true impact of Trump’s tariffs, it is crucial to understand the magnitude of trade between the U.S. and the three countries now subject to trade distortions. For years  now, US trade has been dominated by Mexico, China, and Canada—with Mexico recently becoming the single largest trade partner to the U.S. 

In 2023 alone, trade between the US and these three countries equaled well over $2.1 trillion. For reference, there are only 10 countries in the world with GDPs larger than the trade value between the U.S. and its three largest partners.

In the figure below, we plotted the total imports and exports between the U.S. and China, Mexico, and Canada. As the figure shows, the U.S. runs considerable trade deficits with all three countries. Mexico is the largest trade partner with imports valued at over $475bn and exports valued at over $322bn. It’s followed by Canada with imports valued at $418.6bn and exports valued at $354.3bn. China takes the third position with imports valued at $426.8bn and exports valued at $147.7bn.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/A6nPK/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Using the numbers above, we can calculate the impact of Trump’s recently imposed tariffs using some simple math. After all, tariffs are a tax charged on all imports to a country. So, a 25% tariff on Mexican products will result in tax revenues equivalent to 25% of all Mexican imports. The one caveat to note is the distinction between energy imports and all other goods when it comes to U.S. trade with Canada. But this can be addressed easily noting that Canadian energy exports to the U.S. equaled some $3.2bn in 2023.

Taking this into consideration, we can graph the impact of Trump tariffs by country in the figure below. As we can see, but together, the Trump tariffs would result in impacts of up to $308.36bn. Mexico would be the most affected, with tariffs totaling $118.8bn, followed by Canada with $104.17bn, and China with $85.38bn. 

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/eOCBB/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The problem here is that tariffs are often followed with price distortions. In sum, companies increase the price of their goods by the equivalent increase in tariffs to make up for lost revenues. This, in turn, results in an increase in costs to consumers or, more specifically, an increase in inflation for US consumers. Since US GDP was recently valued at $27.72T, an increase in the costs of goods of $308.36bn would result in a total increase of inflation of about 1.11%. That is, the Trump tariffs are likely to have a direct impact on everyday U.S. citizens in the form of increased prices.

This, of course, is not counting the retaliatory tariffs announced by the governments of China, Mexico, and Canada—which, in turn, would distort the prices of U.S. goods in their respective markets. Using the above data for U.S. exports, we were able to plot the expected impact from corresponding tariffs by China, Mexico, and Canada. As shown in the figure below, Canada would be the most affected with distortions of up to $88.59bn, followed by Mexico with distortions of $80.69bn, and China with $29.56bn.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/l7V6T/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

It didn’t take long for Trump’s tariffs to have a meaningful impact on financial markets. In the figure below, we plotted the value of the S&P 500 over the last month, with a clear downwards trend towards the end of the month—though this could be a result of other financial processes as well as the Trump administration’s harsh meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky. However, it is hard to deny that the recent fall from 5,9549 points to 5,849.72 was mostly the result of president Trump’s tariff announcement. In all, over the last month, the value of the S&P 500 has fallen by 3.1%. 

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/wMujW/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

It remains unclear whether President Trump intends to keep these tariffs across his administration or if he will withdraw them in the near future. For the meantime, they are a clear signal of changing political and economic interests. Companies should take these changing political circumstances into consideration when planning their supply chains and import/export operations.

At Desteia, we believe logistics operators should have all the necessary information to assess the impact of tariffs on their supply chain. If you’d like to see how increased visibility can help you understand the impact of a changing world, make sure to schedule a call with our team of experts.

item.title: Best Supply Chain Visibility Software for 2025
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.content:encoded:
Supply chain visibility software is designed to make your processes more efficient. 

It helps you track shipments, and optimize logistics workflows, supporting your business operation. With this tool, you can reduce administrative load and stay up-to-date to make informed business decisions.

In this blog, I have reviewed the top three best supply chain visibility software solutions in 2025. Here, you'll learn what to look for in a supply chain app and how to pick the best option for your business.

How to Choose the Best Supply Chain Visibility Software

Supply chain tracking software plays a crucial role in inventory visibility. It gives users real-time tracking and management tools to keep an accurate stock of inventory while keeping an eye on operations to avoid mishaps.

Currently, there are dozens of software solutions available in the market. But choosing the right one for your company can be a complicated effort. That is why, we put together this essay, outlining some common trends in supply chain visibility software, what to look for, and some of the main providers.

As a start, if you need some initial suggestions, here are a few things you can do to find the best supply chain visibility software:

  • Identify Needs: Make a list of what is currently missing from your operations – think if you need features like real-time tracking or better inventory management.

  • Check Scalability: Choose an app that can support growing businesses—you don’t want to be stuck with a tool for niche businesses.

  • Integration Options: Ensure the software works with your current tools like ERP or CRM systems.

  • Ease of Use: Pick a user-friendly platform to boost team productivity

  • Real-Time Updates: Opt for real-time visibility providers to avoid delays—many solutions could have considerable lags between a milestone and actual reporting.

  • Vendor Support: Search for customer service with positive feedback.

  • Compare Costs: Compare pricing to get the best deals.

What to Look for in Supply Chain Visibility Software

Finding the right supply chain tracking software can be a tiresome process that involves comparing a number of solutions available in the market. That is why, you should always explore review sites for actual testimonies from users while noting down the best tools and checking their core features and support. Some platforms might offer great smart tools to reduce your administrative workload and some may provide excellent integrations. Perhaps, you need one that does both. 

In the end, choosing the best supply chain software will be a result of your company’s needs. But, in general, there are some key attributes most companies look for when buying supply chain software.

Below are the few key features that you should look for in supply chain visibility software;

Real-Time Tracking and Transparency

With this we mean that the product can track shipments without any considerable delays. It also implies that the company offers full visibility of logistics process relevant to your company .

Reliable Customer Support

A platform that provides 24/7 support with a good response time to help you troubleshoot problems on time. No software is perfect—and few are intuitive—so having that extra support is crucial.

Data Recovery and Integration

The platform you chose should have secure data storage and recovery options in case of any emergency. Moreso in countries where auditing is a common practice, you want to ensure all data provided to a product can be retrieved with ease. Not to mention the need for a smooth integration with existing systems that takes little time and effort—you don’t want to be stuck for months with lengthy integrations.

Customizable Dashboards and Reports

Since all industries might differ slightly, you ultimately want a tool that allows you to personalize dashboards and reports. Think of it as making the most of a tool for you specific use case. In the end, you want to use a single supply chain visibility tool and customization might be a part of it. 

Predictive Analytics

For companies interested in reducing the impact of delays, it is essential that supply chain visibility tools go beyond tracking. This means taking past data and using it to anticipate potential risks or disruptions. With such predictions, operators could prepare well in advance for any potential crisis. 

Multi-Modal Transportation Support

Try to find a tool that supports multiple forms of transportation if that is specific to your use case. Different providers might have specialties in particular forms of transportation, so make sure you get one that aligns to your needs.

Alerts and Notifications

Search for a solution that will not only give you visibility, but will also provide you with alerts and notifications whenever an event seems to impact your supply chain. You want a tool that will tell what is happening and how it impacts your business.

Scalability

SMEs are different to large companies which are different to corporations. If you are a company aiming to grow, make sure that the software solution you are looking for can accommodate for increased volumes and is compliant with tools often used by large enterprises. 

Collaboration Tools

Supply chain visibility tools should, ideally, provide you with an environment where multiple actors in a company can interact with one another. Think of a place where purchasing can look at POs while tracking looks for containers, and planning is getting a real time view of what materials are incoming. You want a product that incentivizes work between departments, making logistics a tool for communication instead of a black box.

Ease of Use

Niche software—like that used in the supply chain industry— is often intricate and difficult to explain to operators. You want to minimize those complexities and find a tool that can deliver on its promises with smooth user interface.

Compliance and Security

Finally, and perhaps most important, you need to have a tool that follows industry standards and adheres to any existing regulations. Your data is a extremely valuable and you want to partner with a product that recognizes its value and relevance. Make sure the product you chose takes the needed precautions to protect your data and avoid any risks to your company or your clients.

Top 3 Supply Chain Visibility Softwares

 1. Desteia

Desteia is a real-time visibility platform that simplifies supply chain management by offering meaningful insights on current operations with a seamless system integration. The product is used by large companies with a specific focus on US-Mexico Trade.

What makes Desteia the best option is its ability to turn existing data from communication outlets (such as emails or text messages) into useful information for logistics operators. A company just needs to connect Desteia to its communication outlets and the product will start receiving documentation and relevant information. Using AI, it then extracts relevant information from those documents to provide real time updates on the status of cargo as well as performance analytics of current carriers or logistics operators. No complicated or lengthy integrations are needed.

Overall, Desteia helps companies make informed decisions, improve operational efficiency, and gain greater control over their supply chain processes.

Pros:

1.  Live Tracking: Desteia enables users to see real time updates on the status of their cargo.

2. Simple Setup: The product is design to be integrated with ease, requiring a much shorter implementation than existing alternatives..

3. High Security: Desteia was designed with security as a top priority, going to great lengths to protect and store customer data in the safest manner possible. 

4. Insight Driven: By gathering useful insights from existing communication outlets, Desteia becomes a powerhouse of insights that will help  yo0u choose the best carriers and routes, thus building a more resilient supply chain.

Cons:

1. Information access: Desteia is designed to tap into existing documents and information sources which might require an additional conversation with a compliance office—although, Desteia’s extensive security policies help assure clients that their data will be managed with care.

2. Project44

Project44 is an established tool in the supply chain world that focuses on providing end to end visibility, from the factory where products are made to the warehouse they are stored in. However, it is known to be complicated to use and carries with it a hefty price tag.

Pros:

1. Advanced Visibility: Within its network of approved carriers, Project44 has great shipment visibility.

2. Trusted Tool: Currently, over 1,000 companies use Project44 to track their shipments.

Cons:

1. High cost: Known to cost 3x as much as established alternatives.

2. Integration Difficulties: Connects to a network of approved carriers—often requiring lengthy implementations to your system.  If your carriers are outside of Project44’s network, implementation can take much longer.

3. Go Comet

Go Comet is a visibility platform that provides multimodal visibility to clients, focusing mostly on large organizations that engage in international trade. 

It is known to be a more complicated product to implement, requiring a number of integrations to a company’s operations. Yet, in return, it delivers users with visibility on port performance and saturation that help identify crises in real time.

Pros:

1. Multimodal capabilities: Offers visibility on all major forms of transportation

2. Market Intelligence: Connected to a number of external sources that help identify global patterns.

3. Real Time Port Visibility: Has great coverage for port saturation and other similar disruptions.

Cons:

1. Lengthy Integration: Many users speak of lengthy integrations that require considerable time to process.

2. Learning Curve: You and your team might require extensive training to take full advantage of the tool.

How to Choose Your Best Alternative?

Picking the best supply chain visibility software is a crucial important decision to ensure smooth business operations. With the right tool, you can avoid delays, maintain operational transparency, and make better business decisions. Desteia stands out as a comprehensive solution, offering real-time insights, and the ability to streamline supply chains effectively. The platform's real-time tracking and delay predictions helped the company identify and address issues early. As a result, they achieved faster deliveries and higher customer satisfaction.

item.title: Supply Chain Bottlenecks: Causes, Solutions and Pro Tips
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.content:encoded:
Supply chain bottlenecks are an unavoidable reality of modern logistics. In order to meet the needs of consumers or manufacturers and provide them with the products that they require, all the links in a supply chain must be effective. The problem is that such processes are often plagued with disruptions which, in many cases, are related with bottlenecks. That is, areas of inefficiency or delay in the system that limit your ability to expand a given process. 

If left unchecked, supply chain bottlenecks can cause various adverse effects, such as cost escalation, customer dissatisfaction, and lost business opportunities. In this article, we explore the concept of supply chain bottlenecks with care, as well as the causes of such bottlenecks, and the ways to overcome them.

Understanding Supply Chain Bottlenecks

A supply chain bottleneck can be described as any factor that inhibits the free flow of goods, information or processes in a supply chain. Just like a traffic congestion in a busy highway, a supply chain also hinders the smooth flow of products and materials while raising the cost of production.

Bottlenecks are often found in the places where there are concerns about capacity, resources, or processes to manage existing loads. Crucially, we should note that supply chain disruptions—the common consequence of bottlenecks—can occur at any stage such as in production, warehousing, transportation or delivery.

Supply Chain Bottleneck Example

Take, for instance,  the semiconductor scarcity that began in 2020. This situation came about due to the  rise in the demand for electronics and the COVID-19 pandemic which made it difficult for effective and timely delivery of these crucial raw materials. Since a company needs to invest huge amounts of resources to increase the output of semiconductors, the existing manufacturing capabilities become a bottleneck when demand grew to such a degree. Even if people wanted to buy semiconductors, there was a physician limitation to how many could be produced.  This soon had an effect on other sectors. As a result, car and tech manufacturers had to slow down their production lines with the likes of Toyota cutting down its worldwide vehicle production by 40 percent because they lacked chips to meet demand—an experience that showed how one constraint impacts many sectors. Thus, bottlenecks early in a supply chain can have great impacts in later stages.

6 Causes for Bottlenecks in Supply Chain

Given how disruptive these issues can be, it is important to identify bottlenecks and understand the causes behind them in order to find the best solution to the problem. 

Though bottlenecks will likely differ by company and sector, below we include some of their most prevalent causes:

1. Natural Disasters

Various natural disasters like earthquakes, floods, and hurricanes are capable of disrupting infrastructure crucial to trade, thus inhibiting production cycles, by bringing transportation systems to a halt. For instance, the 2011 earthquake and tsunami that hit Japan disrupted supply chains worldwide particularly in the automobile and electronics sectors.

2. Labor Shortages

Inadequate workforce or strikes by workers with skills can hamper production and delivery processes. Last year, for instance, east coast port workers went on strike demanding higher wages for their labor. This caused a major supply chain disruption until a settlement was reached.

3. Trade Restrictions

Tariffs, embargoes, and other trade barriers can also cause bottlenecks since they hinder the smooth flow of goods across borders and discourage companies from exporting their products. These have become a common topic of conversation during the second Trump administration, which has used tariffs as a common policy tool when engaging with other countries.

4. Changes in Customer Demand

Changes in consumer behavior or spikes in demand are also known to create bottle necks by causing additional stress to supply chains. These are most common in periods like the holidays where demand for goods tends to increase or when  new trends in the market result in increased consumption of a good. Think, for instance, about the increased demand for e-commerce during the COVID-19 pandemic which led to a strain in the delivery systems.

5. Inventory Forecasting Errors

Stockouts—or ordering too little of a good to meet demand—are the consequences of mis-forecasting the demand which, in turn, affects supply chains in companies around the world. In particular, stockouts lead to delay in order fulfillment and create a bottleneck at inventory management stages.

6. Transportation and Logistics Challenges

These include delays in shipping, congestions at the port, or lack of sufficient transport to move the goods. Basically, any complication in the actual movement of goods—which can be rather common in the logistics instance. The prime example was the 2021 Suez Canal blockage generated by a vessel colliding against one of the walls of the canal. The blockade, in turn, halted global trade for weeks.

8 Strategies to Solve Bottlenecks

Mitigating supply chain constraints is a matter of taking preventive action, investing in new systems, and planning ahead. While the specifics will likely differ by company, we decided to make a list of some effective strategies to overcome such challenges:

1. Improve Inventory Forecasting

Effective inventory forecasting will help you manage the right stock levels to meet the needs of your business without congesting the storage or depleting the necessary stock. AI tools can increase the efficiency of these processes and decrease the margin of error when it comes to forecasting demand patterns.

2. Analysis of the Data and Determination of the Root Causes.

Through analysis of data collected from operations, companies can determine the causes of their bottlenecks in supply chain operations. For instance, if the delays are arising in a certain link in the chain, then further scrutiny of the data may reveal that the issue could be attributed to resource constraint, inefficiency, or outside influences.

3. Promote Supply Chain Process Mapping

Mapping your supply chain makes it possible to have an understanding of the entire processes needed to produce a product from the beginning to the last stage. This visualization assists businesses in recognizing their vulnerable areas and thus prevent inefficiencies from worsening once they arise. It also helps you understand how constraints in one point of the supply chain might result in delays further down the line.

4. Analyze Demand Patterns

This is important in order to prevent bottlenecks. Historical data and predictive analytics can help organizations understand when traffic surges are most likely to occur and make changes to their operations. Such visibility could allow companies to hire additional employees ahead of a peak season or sourcing the needed materials to meet demand.

5. Create Effective Capacity Planning

Capacity planning is the process of matching human and material resources with the forecasted demand. This proactive approach helps in avoiding overloading or underloading of resources hence avoiding any bottlenecks and often relies on the accurate data mentioned on the previous step—think of it as gathering data and then allocating the resources to avoid congestion.

6. Work with Suppliers and Partners

Developing good relationships with suppliers and logistic partners is crucial in enhancing the flow of communication and thus prevent delays and identify any constraints that may be encountered. This will allow your company to have further clarity when disruptions do happen, giving you as much time as possible to find alternative solutions.

7. Embrace Technology and Automation

The use of automated systems and technologies like WMS and TMS can help in minimizing errors that come with manual handling of the operations and fasten the process of solving bottlenecks. These, in turn, could help operate a supply chain much longer than if it were operated solely by humans.

8. Diversify Supply Sources

Using a single supplier or a single region makes the supply chain more prone to disruptions. Having a variety of suppliers and sourcing methods can help to open up other possibilities in the event of a breakdown. Simply put, when a supplier faces a bottleneck, you’ll be able to relly on another to meet your demand.

Tips to Navigate Bottlenecks

Addressing bottlenecks is challenging—there really is no sugar cutting it. That’s why we put together the following tips that can help businesses prepare and respond effectively to various bottleneck items:

Analyze and Rank Constraints

Not all risks are equal. Determine which constraints are the most significant and have the highest effect on your operations. This can help you allocate resources into the areas that could have the most impact to your company.

Plan for Possible Scenarios

Create business continuity plans that address probable scenarios like natural disasters, shortage of workforce, or transportation problems. Scenario planning helps companies be ready to act fast and in the right manner once a crisis does emerge.

Map Your Supply Chain

It is crucial to keep your supply chain map updated to ensure that all the components are captured, and thus, any potential constraints are identified early enough. This will also allow you to see how and where particular disruptions have an impact.

Leveraging Internal Data for Decision Making

Internal data can be used to track KPIs and get valuable information for the improvement of business processes. At times, a low performance of a KPI could indicate the likelihood of a disruption from happening. Make sure to understand all your KPIs and internal data sources to identify potential disruptions.

Promote Collaboration Between Teams

By promoting collaboration between departments and supply chain partners, it is easier to identify and solve issues that may be causing a hold up. Once crises appear, your teams will be able to work together across various business units to find the best solution.

Measure Bottlenecks with Metrics and Data

Current supply chain issues are complex and need a more analytical approach. AI-powered platforms like Desteia offer tools to identify and resolve bottlenecks efficiently by identifying insights in your day. Through metrics like lead times, carrier performance, and route efficiency, Desteia helps companies to identify the bottlenecks and introduce specific solutions.

To learn more about how Desteia can enhance your supply chain, make sure to schedule a demo. Our experts will gladly show you the functionality of our product!

FAQ

1. What is an example of a bottleneck supplier?

A bottleneck supplier is a supplier which is unable to meet customer demands because of constraints in capacity, speed, or resources. For example, a single source of a particular part that is essential in the production process can cause a supply chain breakdown due to production delay.

2. How to overcome a bottleneck?

To get rid of a bottleneck, one has to first understand the cause of the problem, make changes to the process, and purchase equipment to improve throughput. Working with partners and preparing for the unexpected are also very important. But, the specifics will differ with each use case.

3. What are the signs that can help the manager to determine bottlenecks in the production process?

The areas that are likely to cause bottlenecks in the production process can be measured using cycle time, throughput, and resource utilization. Areas of the process where there is evidence of frequent delays or inefficiency should be considered a bottleneck.

Therefore, it is crucial for organizations to identify and tackle these supply chain constraints in order to minimize gaps and enhance management of supply chain operations in the current volatile market environment. Preparedness, evidence-based approaches, and the utilization of innovative solutions are crucial to address these challenges effectively.

item.title: Warehouse vs Distribution Center Explained
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.content:encoded:
Warehouses and distribution centers are crucial elements of modern supply chains. These terms, however, are often a subject of confusion. Although they are often used interchangeably, they serve distinct functions within the logistics process—both of which are crucial for companies. In this article, we’ll explore the differences and similarities between warehousing and distribution, their roles in the supply chain, and how each contributes to the overall efficiency of logistics operations.

What Is a Warehouse?

A warehouse is a facility used primarily for the storage of finished goods. Warehousing and distribution play a vital role in keeping products safe until they’re ready for the next stage in the supply chain. They offer a controlled environment for long-term storage, making them essential for businesses with large inventories or those that need product storage in bulk.

Main Types of Warehouses

  • Public Warehouses: These are owned and operated by third-party companies and are available for rent to businesses that need storage space.

  • Private Warehouses: These warehouses are owned and operated by companies to store their own goods. Large retailers often have private warehouses for their inventory.

  • Distribution Warehouses: These are similar to public warehouses but are more focused on receiving finished goods and storing them for a relatively short time.

  • Climate-Controlled Warehouses: These facilities are designed to maintain a specific temperature and humidity, making them ideal for sensitive goods like pharmaceuticals, perishable items, or electronics.

Why Are Warehouses Important?

Warehouses are important because they provide:

  • Safe Storage: Goods are protected from environmental factors, damage, or theft while kept in storage.

  • Inventory Control: Warehouses allow businesses to track and manage inventory more efficiently. If you want to dive deeper into inventory strategies, check out our article on demand cycles.

  • Buffer for Supply Chain Fluctuations: A warehouse helps businesses adjust to supply and demand shifts by holding extra stock when necessary. In the event of a crisis, these can be used to meet demand until operations are restored back to normal.

What Is a Distribution Center?

A distribution center, on the other hand, is a facility where products are received, stored, and then shipped out to customers or retailers. These centers are critical for businesses that require quick order fulfillment and efficient warehouse distribution processes.

Different Types of Distribution Centers

  • Consolidation Centers: These centers focus on receiving goods from different suppliers and combining them into a single shipment to be delivered to a specific destination. 

  • Break-Bulk Centers: These centers break down large shipments into smaller units, which are then distributed to various locations or retailers.

  • Cross-Docking Facilities: Cross-docking allows goods to be directly transferred from one vehicle to another, reducing the time products spend in storage.

Why Are Distribution Centers Important?

Distribution centers play a critical role in the supply chain for a plethora of reasons. In particular, we can highlight two of them:

  • Speed of Delivery: They enable faster movement of products, ensuring the end customer receives their orders on time. For more on how shipping efficiency impacts your business, and how the choice of a container can have an impact on your product, explore our guide on shipping containers.

  • Cost Efficiency: By optimizing shipping routes and consolidating deliveries, distribution centers help companies reduce shipping costs.

Warehouse vs Distribution Center – Key Differences

While both warehouses and distribution centers handle goods, their functions are quite different. Understanding these distinctions is important for businesses that want to streamline their logistics operations. Let’s dive into the key differences.

1. Operations

  • Warehouse Operations: Warehouses primarily handle long-term storage. Goods are stored in bulk and may sit for extended periods before being moved out—think, again, of stock being kept in case of an emergency or disruption.

  • Distribution Center Operations: In distribution centers, the focus is on speed. Goods are processed quickly, packed, and shipped out to their final destination as fast as possible.

2. Technology and Equipment

  • Warehouse Technology: Warehouses often use inventory management systems (IMS) to keep track of stock levels and optimize storage.

  • Distribution Center Technology: Distribution centers employ advanced technology, including automated sorting systems, conveyor belts, and RFID tracking, to speed up order fulfillment centers.

3. Main Functions

  • Warehouse Function: A warehouse’s main function is to store goods for long periods, providing safe, climate-controlled environments.

  • Distribution Center Function: A distribution center’s main role is to receive, process, and distribute goods quickly and efficiently.

4. Packaging

  • Warehouse Packaging: Products are typically not packaged in a warehouse unless they are specifically needed for storage. Goods are stored in their original packaging or large quantities.

  • Distribution Center Packaging: In distribution centers, goods are often repackaged or prepared for shipping. Products may be individually boxed or grouped together for shipment.

5. Storage

  • Warehouse Storage: Warehouses store large quantities of goods for an extended period. Consider that, when it comes to a warehouse, products might not be moved for weeks or months.

  • Distribution Center Storage: In a distribution center, storage is more temporary, and products are only stored for a short time before being shipped out.

6. Order Fulfillment

  • Warehouse Fulfillment: While warehouses may fulfill orders, it’s not their primary role. Order fulfillment in a warehouse is typically for bulk or large orders.

  • Distribution Center Fulfillment: Distribution centers are designed for quick and efficient order fulfillment, ensuring that products reach their final destination as quickly as possible.

Similarities Between Warehouse and Distribution Center

Although warehouses and distribution centers have distinct functions, they share several important similarities. To start, both are integral parts of an effective supply chain management process for large companies, and both help businesses manage inventory and fulfill end customer orders efficiently. But, more specifically, we can highlight the following similarities between them:

1. Inventory Management

Both warehouses and distribution management centers use inventory systems to track stock, helping businesses stay organized and reduce the risk of stockouts or overstocking. This could be in the form of an integration that tracks purchase orders, bills of lading, and  proforma invoice or through tools more specifically designed to manage inventory.

2. Essential for Supply Chains

Without warehouse management and distribution management centers, it would be nearly impossible to manage large inventories and fulfill customer orders on time. They serve as the backbone of modern supply chains, ensuring goods are always available when needed.

3. Optimize Logistics Operations

Both facilities aim to streamline logistics operations. Warehouses store goods efficiently, while distribution networks ensure that products are processed and shipped quickly. Together, they optimize the entire supply chain.

4. Customer Satisfaction Driven

Both warehouse management systems and distribution centers work to enhance customer satisfaction. Warehouses help ensure that products are available, while distribution centers ensure timely deliveries.

Optimize Your Supply Chain

Understanding the difference between a warehouse and a distribution center is key to optimizing your supply chain. By choosing the right type of facility for your needs, you can improve inventory management systems, reduce costs, and enhance customer satisfaction. Proper planning and transparency in the logistics process ensure that goods move smoothly and efficiently from the supplier to the customer.

In today’s fast-paced business environment, optimizing supply chains is more important than ever before. Whether you’re managing warehouse or distribution services, ensuring that your logistics operations are efficient, cost-effective, and responsive to customer demand is crucial for success.

FAQ

What is 3PL warehousing and distribution?

3PL (Third-Party Logistics) warehousing and distribution channels refer to outsourcing the management of warehousing and distribution activities to a third-party provider. These companies offer efficient storage facilities and order fulfillment services, allowing businesses to focus on core operations while relying on experts for logistics needs.

What are the main types of warehouses?

The main types of warehouses include public warehouses, private warehouses, distribution warehouses, and climate-controlled warehouses. Each type serves different storage needs based on the business's requirements.

What are the 4 types of distribution?

The four types of distribution include:

  1. Direct Distribution: Goods are shipped directly from manufacturer to customer.

  2. Wholesale Distribution: Goods are sold in bulk to retailers.

  3. Drop Shipping: Goods are shipped directly from a supplier to the customer.

  4. Cross-Docking Distribution: Goods are transferred from one vehicle to another without being stored.

item.title: How Mexico Impacts the U.S.
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.description: Mexico is the largest trade partner to the US. We looked at just how much the country influences the US economy and politics.
item.content:encoded:
There is likely no trade relation quite like that of US and Mexico—and 2024 is the year to prove it. The two countries share one of the largest borders in the world and, for years, they’ve adapted their economies to one another. The relationship is so vast that last year, Mexico finally surpassed China as the largest trade partner to the US—despite having 9% of the population of China, and an economy basically a tenth in size.

To put it plainly, Mexico is the largest trade partner to the largest economy in the world. Their trade relation, in turn, is one of the most important to the modern economy. However, when we speak of the US-Mexico relation, we often focus on the impact the former has on the latter—namely, just how much the US impacts Mexico’s economy. Yet, given how large trade between the two economies is, one can only expect for Mexico to have a proportional impact on the U.S. economy.

In this essay, we turn the common focus of this relation on its head. Instead of looking at how the US impacts Mexico—which, it does—we focus on how Mexico impacts the U.S. Namely, how much does Mexico weigh in the U.S. economy and how these impacts are spread across the country.

I. The Proportion of Impact

Let’s start by addressing the elephant in the room. It is true that the relationship between Mexico and the U.S. is disproportionate—such could be expected given that the U.S. economy is 15 times that of Mexico. In the figure below, we plotted Mexico’s 2023 exports according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC) by the destination country. As the figure shows, a full 75.76% of all Mexican exports are headed to the U.S. Canada, the second largest export destination for Mexico, only accounts for 5.4% of exports from Mexico. 

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/13rNY/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The same, however, is not true of the U.S. In the next figure, we plotted the origin of US imports for the same year. Mexico is the largest trade partner to the U.S.—that much is true. But the totality of Mexican exports to the country account for just 15.2% of U.S. imports. A number which is close to the share of U.S. imports from China (14.5%) and Canada (13.6%).

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/CMJKN/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Yet even if the relationship is skewed, it is still a booming relationship. One that, in fact, has grown to great proportions in recent years as the U.S. seeks to shift supply chains away from China—a pattern shared by various developed economies commonly referred to as “nearshoring.” Given Mexico’s existing relationship with the U.S. and close proximity, it has become a natural replacement for China, not to mention the similarity in terms of manufacturing capabilities while keeping lower labor costs.

Given these trends, US-Mexico trade has grown exponentially in recent years. In the figure below, we show Mexico's imports and exports to the U.S. since 2006. In that nearly 20 year period, Mexican imports from the U.S. have grown by 112%. Meanwhile, Mexican exports have grown by 122%. In the same period, both imports and exports have more than doubled between the two countries.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/HeeUB/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

II. Economic Impact

But what’s most interesting is that the impact of this increase in trade with Mexico is not evenly distributed across the U.S. In the following map, we focus on a smaller period between 2019 and 2023. In it, we plotted the change in imports from Mexico by U.S. states. As the figure shows, all but 10 states actually saw considerable increases when it comes to Mexican imports. The largest change, by far, was the state of Delaware with a 268.47% increase in Mexican imports. It was followed by Louisiana (137.5% increase) and Virginia (115.38%).

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BLF8P/2/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

U.S. exports to Mexico, on the other hand, were far more homogenous. In the figure below—replicating the preceding map—we plotted the change in exports to Mexico by US State between 2019 and 2023. Here, Alaska and Oregon saw the largest increases in exports to Mexico with over 1,000% increases each—likely suggesting that trade between these states and Mexico was basically nonexistent beforehand.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/NVJBO/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Now, since the above maps focus on the change of imports and exports, they fail to show just how relevant Mexican trade might be to each state in the U.S. To address this, in the next map we plotted what share of a state’s GDP is equivalent to the value of their specific trade with Mexico. This gives a better idea of how and where Mexico impacts the U.S. 

Not surprisingly, in large states like Texas and California, despite trading millions with Mexico each year, trade with the country accounts for less than 0.001% of GDP—a result of their large economies more than a disregard for Mexico. But, what’s most interesting is how some smaller states depend on Mexico to a large degree. By far, the most dependant states on Mexican trade are New Hampshire, where trade with the country accounts for 1.03% of state GDP, followed by North Dakota (0.97% of state GDP) and South Dakota (0.81%). There is also an interesting geographic concentration in the north west of the US, from Oregon—which, again, saw a drastic increase in exports to Mexico—all the way to Nebraska. Also, an interesting concentration occurs in the three states in the U.S. Northeast (Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont).

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/gO68o/2/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

III. Political Impact

As a form of influence, we were interested in testing if there were any political patterns that resulted from U.S.-Mexico Trade. In particular, if a state’s political tendencies shared any relation with Mexico trade. Since the U.S. has a steady two party system, it is rather straightforward to categorize each state as either red (for republican), blue (for democrat), or purple (for states where margins could favor either party in an election).

We proceeded to calculate the total trade balance for red, blue, and purple states, and plotted them in the figure below. Interestingly, there is quite a difference between political affiliation and whether a state runs a deficit or a surplus. Blue states, as a group, run large surpluses with Mexico—meaning they export more than they import. Red States, on the other hand, run deficits which—namely, they import more than they export from Mexico. Purple states run a smaller surplus.

A similar pattern is true if we look at the average surplus or deficit of Red, Blue and Purple states. The average Blue state runs a $52.6 million surplus with Mexico while Red states run an average deficit of $6.8 million. The one change is that, on average, Purple states do have a larger deficit at $13.9 million—surpassing Red states.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yPePI/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

We wanted to go further on this, so we decided to look at whether the recent increase in trade with Mexico had a noticeable effect on U.S. politics. More specifically, if changes in Mexican trade had any effect on the results of the recent U.S. election—and support to republican candidate, Donald Trump, who ran on a hostile campaign against Mexico.

We found no statistical relationship between the change in Trump vote and the change of Mexican imports or the overall total deficit. However, we did find a statistically significant relationship between the growth in exports and the rise of Trump votes (with a p value of 0.035, below the standard 0.05 threshold for significance). Meaning that in states where exports to Mexico grew between 2020 and 2024, so did support for the Republican party.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/6AWgl/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

In all, this research suggests that Mexico does hold some prominent influence on the U.S. economy. Although it is true that the US influences Mexico to a much larger degree, there are certain states in the union that are particularly sensitive to Mexican trade. Not to mention that the U.S. political landscape has become sensitive to Mexican commerce as we showed in the last section of this essay.

item.title: Maritime Accidents and Incidents: Number, Types and Location
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.description: Maritime incidents are a common phenomena in the world of logistics. In this essay, we quantify just how common they truly are.
item.content:encoded:
Maritime incidents are the bread and butter of the logistics world. After a year like 2024, plagued with disruptions and unforeseen events, operators have grown accustomed to ships encountering problems at sea—be it a hurricane closing ports or pirates attacking cargo ships. The question, however, is how likely it is that any given vessel will be subject to an incident?

Our analysis—which we will examine further in this paper—suggests that around 2.61% of the global shipping fleet today was subject to at least one incident in the last decade. 

But, let’s start with the basics. Ocean incidents, from flooding and collisions to fires and mechanical difficulties, are, indeed, extremely common. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has a thorough registry of all incidents over the last years which we used across this paper to determine the true magnitude of this phenomenon. Just how common are these incidents? Well, over the last decade (between 2015 and 2024) the IMO registered 2,935 incidents at sea. That comes down to about an incident every other day for the period examined—0.8 incidents per day, but, since vessels don’t exist in fractions, we will keep the above statement to be accurate.

We know that, as of 2024, the total number of vessels at sea was an estimate of 109,000—including non-cargo and cargo vessels alike. According to IMO data, the 2,935 incidents registered over the last decade involved 3,352 vessels—of which, 2,849 were unique vessels, thus suggesting there were, at most, 503 vessels with at least two incidents. This, in turn implies that, over the last decade, roughly 2.61% of vessels in the global fleet have suffered at least one accident. 

In the figure below, we plotted the precise location of all maritime incidents over the last decade. The color of each point, as shown in the accompanying legend, indicates whether it was a small incident (Marine Incident), a casualty (Marine Casualty), or a severe incident with casualties (Very serious marine casualty). If you hover your mouse over any figure, it will show further information on the incident, including its date and location.

Maritime Accidents by Severity

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/eOlTW/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Additionally, as one can notice from the color of each dot in the map, there does seem to be a tendency towards very severe incidents. In the pie chart below, we divided the total incidents by their severity. As the figure shows, 61.87% of all incidents in the examined period were considered “very serious marine casualties” by the IMO. These were followed by non-serious casualties (28.96%) and lower-level incidents (9.17%).

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/XsHkI/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

We can further look at geographic data from the IMO to determine the location of each incident relative to existing infrastructure. As we show in the figure below, the bulk of incidents happen out at sea, with 26.31% occurring in open waters, and an additional 24.87% occurring in coastal waters—together accounting for over half of all occurrences. These were, in turn, followed by incidents at port with 18.74% of occurrences.

Maritime Incidents by Location

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/erNCz/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

The IMO also provides important information on the specifics of each incident which allows us to understand the most common issues impacting the global shipping fleet. In the figure below, we plotted each of the official categories registered by the IMO for maritime incidents. As one can see, these categories are extremely specific, giving a more accurate depiction of problems at sea. By far, the most common category was contact with some form of fixed object—ie, a collision—which represents 139 of all incidents over the last decade. These were followed by groundings (85 instances) and occupational incidents (84 occurrences). Although it is worth noting that no single category accounts for over 5% of incidents in the examined period.

Maritime Incidents by Type

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/q01HL/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

It is worth noting that, in recent years, incidents have become less and less common. In the figure below, we plotted the total number of incidents registered in any given year. As we can see from the graph, there has been a sharp decline in incidents since 2017, when the IMO registered the highest number of incidents of the decade: 460. By 2023, the number had fallen to just 236—data for 2024 hasnt been updated since June of that year.

Number of Maritime Incidents per Year

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/zDF3K/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Now that we are speaking of time trends, it is worth digging deeper into IMO data to draw useful conclusions for logistics operators. More specifically, we’d be interested in showing which are the most common dates in which incidents occur. To do so, we designed two graphs which we share below.

First, in the following graph, we divided the incidents observed by the month in which they took place. As the graph shows, there are two important bumps in the data: one in February and one in August. These would roughly align with heavy traffic periods for logistics such as Chinese New Year, and the summer months as companies prepare shipments for the holiday seasons.

Number of Maritime Incidents per Month

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3KmGd/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Second, in the subsequent figure we did the same analysis as above but, instead of disaggregating data by month, we did it by the hour in which an incident was registered. As the figure shows, there is a sharp increase at midnight, which is likely a result of internal records being updated at the end of each day—but that is a mere hypothesis. Besides that drastic increase, we also see considerable peaks around 9 am and 1 pm—which might correlate to busy periods at ports.

Number of Maritime Incidents per Hour

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Y7eA1/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Finally, tapping into one additional element of IMO data, we were able to identify the countries that are most prone to file incidents with the organization. In the map below, the color of each country indicates how many reports each country filled over the last decade. Colors close to purple indicate the country filled more reports with the IMO while those closer to yellow indicate the country filled less reports. As the data shows, Panama was the country that filled the most reports with 187, followed by the UK with 107.

Number of Maritime Incident Investigation Reports by Country

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SxJYf/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

All the information above suggests that maritime incidents are not just common, but are also complicated. They cannot be easily explained by a handful of theories even though, at least in terms of time and location relative to port, they do follow some important patterns. These details should be taken into consideration by operators when planning routes or designing supply chains for a company.

At Desteia, we leverage data similar to that displayed in this article to help operators identify the impact to their specific use cases. If you’d like to see how ocean incidents—and many other variables—could impact your supply chain, make sure to schedule a call with our team:

item.title: Customs Rules and Regulations for Shipping to Mexico
item.dc:creator: Jose Luis Sabau
item.description: We looked at existing data on Mexican customs to identify the busiest months and customs points across the country.
item.content:encoded:
Mexican customs are complicated—and perhaps, such is to be expected when dealing with the 12th largest economy in the world. Just in 2024, the country received over $625 bn worth of goods while sending an additional $617 bn abroad, bringing total trade to well over $1.2T. 

Not to mention that trade with Mexico is growing at an accelerated pace, as countries around the world seek to relocate their supply chains in  a process commonly known as nearshoring. Just between 2023 and 2024, total trade grew by 4.2%, and will likely continue to grow in years to come.

Given the importance of Mexico in international commerce, in this article, we decided to look more closely at one of the key elements in the country’s trade process. Namely, the structure of Mexican customs. More specifically, we looked at which customs points in Mexico are the most important, how they've changed over time and, crucially for operators, when they tend to be at their busiest.

To start, we should note that Mexico has 85 different customs points across the country—that is, places in which foreign cargo can enter the country for revision or domestic cargo can be sent abroad. Of these, 21 are located along the US-Mexico border, 17 at maritime ports, and an additional 12 were in Mexico’s interior—mostly in the form of airports.

The distribution of these customs facilities, however, changes drastically when considering the volumes each handles in a year. Take, for instance, 2023—the latest year for which the Mexican government has released data—. During that year, as shown in the figure below, border customs handled almost 70% of the total customs traffic in Mexico, despite the fact that only 42% of customs facilities are located at the border. These were followed by interior customs points, with 19.1% of all operations and maritime with 11%—a considerable shift since maritime customs points are actually the second most common in Mexico but the third in terms of use.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dbJi8/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

In the figure below, we went further and mapped each of Mexico’s 85 customs points. The size of each circle represents the volume of operations handled in the year 2023. Again, there is great prominence on the US-Mexico border. In fact, the four largest customs points by volume were all located along the border: Nuevo Laredo, Tijuana, Ciudad Juarez, and Reynosa. You can hoover over each dot to see the name of each customs point and their volumes.

[iframe]https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Rykd1/1/|CustomHeight=700px[/iframe]

Over the years, customs operations have grown considerably in Mexico. This, of course, is a result of the booming trade relationship with the US and the growing interest in Mexico across the global economy which has drastically increased the nation’s trade volumes. In the figure below, we show the number of operations every month at all Mexican customs facilities between 2012 and 2023.
